data.title: What to do after Matric, FSc or your degree
data.summary: A simple way to choose between university, a skill, a government job or studying abroad — without paying anyone to decide for you.

steps.title: Start from the goal, not the degree
steps.body: Write down what you want in five years: a profession, a steady income soon, or to live and study abroad. Talk to two people who actually do that work and ask what they wish they had known.

steps.title: Match the goal to its entry route
steps.body: Medicine and dentistry go through MDCAT. Engineering, computer science and business usually go through university entry tests (many accept NTS tests, others run their own). The civil service starts with a Bachelor's degree and then FPSC or provincial commission exams. Skills-first routes include NAVTTC programmes, DigiSkills and diplomas. Studying abroad mostly runs through scholarships.

steps.title: Check that the institution and programme are recognised
steps.body: Before you apply or pay a fee, confirm the university or college is recognised — HEC for universities, PMDC for medical and dental colleges. A glossy brochure is not recognition.

steps.title: Look for money before you look for admission
steps.body: Need-based and merit scholarships open on their own calendars: HEC need-based aid and the Ehsaas undergraduate scholarship, PEEF in Punjab, SEF in Sindh, the LUMS National Outreach Programme, and many universities' own aid. Note the windows now.

steps.title: Build a calendar — and a plan B
steps.body: List every test date and application deadline, add them to your phone's calendar (RAAHI can export deadlines as .ics files), and choose a plan B in the same field in case the first choice does not come through. Use the waiting time to learn a skill for free.

data.duration: One evening to decide, a few weeks to prepare
data.audience: Students finishing Matric, Intermediate or a Bachelor's who are not sure what comes next.
checklist: CNIC, or B-Form if you are under 18
Matric and Intermediate certificates and mark sheets
Income certificate or other proof if you apply for need-based aid
A mobile number and email address you check every day
pitfalls: Paying an ‘admission consultant’ for a guaranteed seat — merit seats are not for sale.
Assuming every private university or college is recognised.
Missing a registration window because you followed dates from social media instead of the official page.
Choosing a field only because your friends did.
